10. The learned Attorney-General contended that since article 15 of the Order is inconsistent or repugnant to, article 109 of the Constitution the superintending power as has been canvassed strenuously both by Mr. Abdur Rahman Chowdhury and Mr. Mainul Hossain, are also not available. The argument in plain language proceeds thus : President's Order No. 50 precludes the challenge of its decision except by appeal, the superintending power under article 109 is not available to challenge that decision because article 47 sub-article (2) says that the inconsistency, if any, between the law and the Constitution the provisions of that law will prevail. To our query to point out the inconsistency the learned Attorney-General contended that article 15 of the PO in clear terms says the tribunal's action or proceeding shall not be called in question. The argument proceeds in circle. In the first schedule of the Constitution a number of PO find mentioned and these Orders were promulgated before the promulgation of the Constitution. The pre-constitutional legislation required a protection otherwise the wires of some of these Orders could be challenged in a Court of law and the framers of the Constitution in their wisdom considered it fit to give protection to these laws in spite of the fact that some of the provisions of some of the laws may be repugnant to or inconsistent with the supreme law, namely, the Constitution. This is a Constitutional device to protect these laws from any possible attack. Otherwise some of the laws may come within the mischief of article 26 of the Constitution. Article 47(2) thus protects these laws or everything done 'under the authority of such law'. But if on facts it transpires that the action taken is not 'under the authority of such law' such action is not protected. This protection was necessitated for the purpose of giving the full opportunity for the development of the society which has been stated as the fundamental aim of the State, namely, to realise through the democratic process a socialistic society free from exploitation a society in which a rule of law, fundament human right and freedom, security, justice, political, economical and, social security for the citizens of Bangladesh can be secured. In order to build up an egalitarian society for which tremendous sacrifice was made by the youth of this country in the national liberation movement, the Constitution emphasises for building up society free from exploitation of man by man so that people may find the meaning of life. After all, the aim of the Constitution is the aim of human happiness. The Constitution is the supreme- law and all laws are to be tested in the touch stone of the Constitution (vide article 7). It is the supreme law because it exists, it exists because the Will of the people is reflected in it. History of mankind is replete with instances when a Constitution ceased to exist because the Will of the people was either not reflected in it or the support was withdrawn ultimately. It is rather late in the day to suggest that a pre-constitutional piece of legislation will displace one of the three structural pillars on which the mechanism of the Constitution rest. flaying declared that parliamentary democracy is the manifest aspiration of the people of Bangladesh, the constitutional instrument has been drafted keeping in full view that the power of three organs of Government, namely. Executive, Legislative and Judiciary are well defined. The learned Attorney General's submission if accepted will result in uncertainty because the administration of justice is the responsibility of the judiciary. The Supreme Court retains its control over the subordinate judiciary by virtue of its power of superintendence and control, a power that has been inherited from the past. As far as back as 1861 this power of superintending was given to the High Court. Clause 15 of the High Court Act, 1861 provided that High Court shall have superintendence over all Courts which may be subject to its appellate .jurisdiction. Section 107 of the Government of Indian Act, 1915 reiterated the same conferment, namely, the High Court will have superintendence over all Courts which are subject to its 'appellate jurisdiction'. It is thus clear both the Act 1861 and the Acts of 1915 conferred the power of superintendence and control over the Courts which were subject to the appellate jurisdiction of the High Court. Subsequences much water had flown from the Himalaya and the Government of India Act, 1935 way promulgated. Article 224 of the 1935 Act provided the power of superintendence over all Courts which were subject to its 'appellate jurisdiction'. Between 1915 and 1935 British had to wage a war, namely the First World War, she had to face the Jalianabag. She was confronted with two kinds of movements, namely. violent and non-violent. The Civil Disobedience Movement of Mahathma Gandhi is a part of the story of the independence movement. A protection was needed from the interference of the judiciary. Special Courts were created and for that purpose sub-article (2) was promulgated taking away the High Court's .jurisdiction to question any judgment of any inferior Court which was not otherwise subject to appeal or revision. This enactment for the first time took away expressly the powers of the High Court. The sub-section (2) of section 224 deprived the High Courts of the revisional powers which they were exercising over Courts subject to their appellate jurisdiction ever since the constitution of High Courts in 1861. Originally under section 15 of the High Courts Act, 1861 and later under section 107 of the Government of Indian Act, 1915. Then in 1947 the Indian Independence Act was promulgated and Pakistan came into existence. In the meantime the Government of India Act, 1935 continued in force in Pakistan after 1947. In 1956 after much labour a Constitution was promulgated in the erstwhile Pakistan. In the third schedule, part II of that Constitution it was provided that the High Court shall have superintendence and control over all Courts subject to its appellate or revisionary jurisdiction. While the 1861 Act and 1915 Act mentioned only the 'appellate jurisdiction' and nothing about the revisionary jurisdiction in 1935 Act the substantial departure was made by expressly providing that he judgment of the inferior Courts which are not otherwise subject to appeal or revision shall not be questioned. In the first flash of independence from the British Government the framers of the Pakistan Constitution of 1956, belatedly though, reconferred the power of superintendence and control over all Courts subject to its appellate or revisionary jurisdiction. In 1958 the Constitution was abrogated but the Laws (Continuance in Force) Order, 1958 by article 2(2) the powers and jurisdiction of the Court were continued. Then in 1962 a Constitution was promulgated and in article 102 it was stated that the High Court shall supervise and control all other Courts that are subordinate to it. The well-known expression 'superintendence' was omitted and in its place a new expression namely 'supervise' was used in this Constitution. Munir (former Chief Justice of Pakisatan) commented on his book on the `Constitution of Islamic Republic of Pakistan' that the terms of article 102 were stronger than those of section 107 of the Government of India Act and they were not subject to the limitation that was introduced by sub-section (2) of section 224 of the 1935 Act. This power `may be used ex debito justitiae, where there is no other remedy available under the ordinary law.' 

 11. Then the 1962 Constitution was abrogated and by the Provisional Constitutional Order, 1969 the power and jurisdiction of the Courts was continued, subject to certain conditions and PO No. 3 of 1969 which specifically laid down that no Court shall question any finding, sentence, order, proceeding or other action of Martial Law Authority. It may be stated that the Courts including the High Court and Supreme Court was at minimum and the question whether the High Court still possessed the superintending power was never mooted. Then came 1971-a period of chaos and confusion. It was the dark period of our national life. It was the brightest period for our existence and the aspiration of the people was fulfilled on 16th day of December, 1971 when the emergence of Bangladesh was established as a fact. It was the brightest period because on the 10th of April, 1971 Declaration of Independence was made and on the same day Laws Continuance Enforcement Order was promulgated. Since then reaction faced revolution and ultimately victors became vanquished. Provisional Constitution, of Bangladesh Order was promulgated on the 11th January, 1972 and the Constituent Assembly as defined in that Order ultimately met and promulgated the Constitution which came in force on the 16th day of December, 1972. Article 109 is mentioned in this Constitution. This survey shows that this power of superintendence has been handed down to this Court since 1861 and except the period during which the Country was under Martial Law in 1958-1962 and 1969-71 the High Court retained the superintending power. It is of no use to speculate now whether during the Martial Law the superintending power was available because the question has become academic. It will be presumed that this power was available to the extinct High Court since the power was not taken away expressly. 

 This significant omission has been regarded by all High Courts in India before whom this question has arisen as having restored to the High Court the power of judicial superintendence it has "under section 15 of the High Courts Act, 1861 and section 107 of the Government of India Act, 1915. See the cases referred to in Moti Lai V The State AIR 1952 at page 966(A). Our attention has not been drawn to any case which has taken a different view and as at present advised, we see no reason to take a different view." 

 30. Now let us consider the cases cited by the learned Attorney-General. The learned Attorney-General cited the case of the Chief Secretary to the Government of East Pakistan vs Moslem-uddin Sikdar reported in (1957) 9 DLR (SC) 20A =PLD 1957 SC page 1. The Dacca High Court considered the vires of the Ordinance No. 12 of 1956. East Pakistan Food (Control of Movement and Distribution) Ordinance. One Abdul Barek Sikdar was tried and convicted under section 6 of the Ordinance. The Dacca High Court without deciding the case on merit considered the vires of sections 11, 12, 13, 14 and 18 as ultra vires and concluded that these sections of the Ordinance were inconsistent with Code of Criminal Procedure and therefore held to be void and concluded "the pretended trial of the prisoner was vitiated with illegality." The East Pakistan Government filed the appeal before the Supreme Court for obtaining a decision regarding the legality of the Ordinance. In the Ordinance section 13 provided "there shall be no appeal from any order or sentence passed by a Special Magistrate, no Court shall have any authority to revise such order or sentence or to transfer any case from the Court of any Special Magistrate." In the face of this clear language the petitioner challenged the conviction by way of writ under article 170 of the Constitution. In this enactment revisional jurisdiction was ousted in express language. It was not challenged by way of superintending power of the High Court. Section 20 of that Ordinance laid down that no order made in the exercise of any power shall be called in question in any Court. The Dacca High Court arrived at the finding that notwithstanding section 20 of the Ordinance just mentioned the petition under article 170 of the Constitution was maintainable. Section 20 was not a bar to the exercise of the jurisdiction under article 170. This view of the Dacca High Court was not challenged before the Supreme Court. Cornelious, J (as his Lordship then was) observed :— 

 31. The next case cited by the learned Attorney-General is the celebrated decision namely Hari Meah vs The State reported in 10 DLR 123. The Dacca Court considered the question of jurisdiction in that case. The petitioner was tried summarily by the Special Magistrate of Comilla under section 6 of the East Pakistan Food (Special Courts) Act X of 1956. The petitioner preferred a criminal revision in the High Court. Hamoodur Rahman, J. (as his Lordship then was) considered the point of maintainability. By that Act X of 1956 Special Court was set up for speedy trial of offences in relations to food-stuff. Section 4 authorised the Government to appoint Special Magistrate. Section 8 provided "that Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, in so far as they are applicable and in so far as they are not inconsistent with the provisions of the Act, shall apply." The Act did not say anything about the appeal or revision. His Lordship in his carefully considered decision observed that no appeal lay to the High Court and then proceeded whether the High Court could interfere in revision in exercise of the powers under section 439 of the CrPC Relying on two decisions namely AIR 1918 Patna 103 and AIR 1943 Patana 18 his Lordship came to the conclusion that the powers that were exercised by the Special Magistrate was conferred on him by the Act itself and his jurisdiction was also a special jurisdiction. Therefore that Court could not be called a Criminal Court inferior to the High Court. It is unfortunate that the attention of his Lordship was not drawn to the fact that the Act itself did not speak of any appeal or revision nor was there any ouster clause as was in sections 13 and 20 of the Ordinance No. 12 of 1956. It was not argued before his Lordship whether the power of superintendence was available. On appeal the Supreme Court of Pakistan in 11 DLR SC 368 decided the issue that there is no right of appeal because the Special Magistrate was not the Magistrate First Class as mentioned in section 408 CrPC The Supreme Court therefore' concluded that the order of the Special Magistrate under the Special Courts Act was not appealable. Significantly the Supreme Court did not proceed further as to whether the revisional jurisdiction was available for interfering with the order of the Special Court. The decision in the High Court in this case is fully correct in view of the provision of section 408 of the CrPC but with greatest respect to the eminent Judge it must be stated that the decisions relied on by him have probably no manner of approach in the facts and circumstances of the law that governed the case. 

 33. Incidentally Mr. Abdur Rahman Chowdhury drew our attention to the observation of Murshed. C.J. in the case of Nurjahan vs The Authorised Officer reported in 17 DLR. Dacca 393. His Lordship considered the East Bengal Construction Act. 1953 and arrived at the conclusion that the Magistrate, First Class trying a case under the East Bengal Building Construction Act does not cease to be a Magistrate under the Code of Criminal Procedure. His Lordship concluded that this Court is a Court under the Code and arrived at the conclusion that the appeal against the decision of such a Magistrate is competent. Thereafter his Lordship observed :— 

 "The Supreme Court of Pakistan in Hari Meah's case reported in 11 DLR SC 368 has merely held under the facts and circumstances of that case that an appeal under section 408 of the Code would not lie and the decision goes no further than that. The revisional jurisdiction of the High Court under section 439 of the Code is much wider." It will be noticed that Murshed, C.J., in this case did not decide the point as his Lordship was not called upon to do so. 

 35. The language of the enactment had expressly took away not only the powers of revision but the jurisdiction of any kind what soever was also taken away. The Full Bench considered this legislation and Dawson Miller, CJ after considering the inherited powers of the High Court since 1861 came to the conclusion as follows :— 

 36. It is clear that the jurisdiction of any kind "was taken away by section 8 of the Ordinance." Therefore the question of superintending and control over the Court of the Commissioners which were created newly by the enactment did not arise because the High Court never exercised such jurisdiction over such Court is the past. Further having taken away the jurisdiction of the High Court it was provided by section 11 of the Act that no order under the Act should be questioned in any Court. The High Court inherited certain jurisdiction since 1861 and unless by express legislation that jurisdiction is taken away interference by the High Court will be called for in appropriate circumstances. Section 8 of that enactment took away all the jurisdiction and then section II provided that no order shall be questioned in any Court. But can it be said that the same consequences will follow in the instant case ? The PO 50/72 was promulgated under the Provisional Constitution of Bangladesh Order. That Constitutional Order created a High Court namely High Court of Bangladesh and subsequently by the PO No. 5 in article 4 it has been expressly said that the High Court shall have powers in respect of territories of Bangladesh, all such original, appellate, special, revisional, review, procedural and all other powers as were exerciseable in respect of the said territories by High Court at Dacca under any law inforce before the 26th of March, 1971. In the proviso certain powers of the extinct High Court at Dacca were expressly taken away namely the powers of issuance of writ. The territories of Bangladesh are same as it was on the 26th of March, 1971 and for this geographical area only one Court was created, namely the High Court of Bangladesh and. as such the High Court's power that was in existence prior to 26th March, 1971 was preserved by the Provisional Constitutional Order and by the Constitution itself vide paragraph 6(5) of the Fourth Schedule. 

 38. It is thus clear that the Full Bench although did not exercise the power of revision but exercised the power under section 491 and the petitioner was set at liberty at once on the ground that case was not covered by Ordinance itself. These two decisions were relied on in Hari Meah's case. It is unfortunate that it was not brought to the notice of his Lordship Harnoodur Rahman, J. that in the case of AIR 1918 Patna page 303, section 8 expressly took away all the jurisdiction and in the case of AIR 1943 Patna 18 section 26 provided for one appeal only to the Special Judge and took away all other jurisdiction including section 491 CrPC. Notwithstanding this exclusion the Court released the petitioners on the ground that the case was not covered by the Ordinance Because it did not apply. The enactment that was considered by his Lordship Hamoodur Rahman, J in 10 DLR. Dacca, namely, East Pakistan Special Act X of 1956 did not contain any such ouster clause of jurisdiction. By no means it should be construed that we are taking different view from the law laid down in Hari Meah's case. On the contrary we are in respectful agreement with his Lordship's decision. We are only pointing out that the absence of ouster clause of jurisdiction was neither pointed out to his Lordship nor the power of superintending and control was raised before his Lordship. In the instant case both Mr. Abdur Rahman Chowdhury and Mr. Mainul Hosein urged the power of superintendence and control and the learned Attorney-General joined the issue. We shall deal with this aspect of the Constitutional point at the appropriate place. 

 A person who can commit a person to custody performs a judicial function. In the case of Aiustaq Ahmed vs State reported in 17 DLR (SC) 624 a learned Judge of the Lahore High Court was on an inspection tour and while inspecting, he found that one Mustaq Ahmed was abusing the liberty allowed to him by the learned Sessions Judge who released him on bail.  87. The learned Attorney General then cited the case of Ghulam Muhammad vs Muzammal Khan reported in 19 DLR (SC) 439, in support of his contention that the proceeding should not be quashed at this stage. In that case a Single Judge of the Lahore High Court quashed the proceedings U/S 561A, CrPC because the High Court thought that it was not the business of the police to submit any chalan for the commission of offence not disclosed in the FIR. What happened is this: The shareholders of the Mechanical Himalaya Transport Company Limited were divided into two Groups known respectively as the Batala Broup and the Jammu and Kashmir Group. Eventually Ghulam Muhammad belonging to the Jammu and Kashmir group was appointed as an agent or a lessee to run the business of the company. He then took custody of the vehicle and other assets of the company in pursuance of the said decision. The appellant relying upon the resolution of the 14th August, 1957 filed a complaint with the police alleging that one Afsar Khan who was appointed as a Manager by him after taking over the management of the company had committed criminal breadeh of trust. On this complaint the police started investigation and discovered a large number of other instances of criminal breach of trust by the employees and other office bearers of the company to cover which they had also committed forgeries for the purpose of cheating the company. The police filed three separate chalans. But no chalan was, however, submitted to the police in respect of the offence that was alleged in the FIR nor any final report was filed in respect thereof. The Additional District Magistrate ultimately framed three separate charges, one against the respondent Muzammal Khan, Afsar Khan and Mohammad Hafeez under sec. 468 PC and another against Afsar Khan, Muzammal Khan and Lal Din U/S 468/109 and the third against five persons, namely, Afsar Khan, Muzammal Khan, Fazal Hussain, Lal Din and Mohammad Ashraf U/S 468 PC. three separate petitions were filed in the High Court U/S 561A, CrPC and the High Court after hearing the same, quashed all the three proceedings. Then the matter came before the Supreme Court and the Supreme Court observed that if the evidence against the respondents disclosed a prima facie case, then justice clearly requires that the trial should proceed according to law. The fact that weighed with their Lordships was that the mere fact that a long period had expired since an initiation of the proceeding is no ground for quashing the criminal proceeding. In this context the Supreme Court observed :— 

 89. Now let us consider whether we are stifling the criminal prosecution. The learned Attorney-General cited the decision in the case of Raja Haq Nawaz vs Mu-Muhammad Afzal reported in (1967) 19 DLR (SC) 69=PLD 1967 (SC) 354 In this case leave to appeal was granted for considering whether quashment of the proceeding at the complaint stage was justified. It was pointed out before Court that the conclusion of and the learned Chief justice of the High Court that the allegations of cheating, house trespass and intimidation were totally false was open to criticism on the point of sufficiency and even accuracy. From the plain reading of the report it appears that the High Court was not correct on the factual position. The Supreme Court granted leave to appeal and observed:— 

 91. Now we come to the other aspect of this point, namely quashing of the proceeding. We have given our anxious consideration to this aspect of the case because if the offence is committed, that offence must be investigated and the culprit must be punished. PO 50/72 has been characterised as harsh law and the learned Attorney-General asked us to take into consideration the contemporaneous facts and Mr. Abdur Rahman Chowdhury at once accepted the suggestion of the learned Attorney-General, although for a different reason, viewing it from a different angle. It is not for us say to whether the law is harsh or not. But as we find in the preamble of the law in question it runs to the effect that "it is expedient to make special provision for the suppression of certain offences of a grave nature". It may be noted that in Act X of 1956 which was the subject-matter of the case of Hari Mea [11 DLR (SC) 368) the preamble was to the effect that 

 94. When all the three ingredients are present the illustration says that Z has committed the mischief. In the instant case the first ingredient is present, namely, the insurance was there. But the second and the third ingredient are totally absent. No voluntary action on the part of Mridha has been alleged nor any abetment on his part has been shown on facts. Nor has it been proved satisfactorily how he gained by the fire. He has another godown within 20 yards of the place where he had substantial stock of jute. But it was not gutted by fire. It is not disputed by the State that Mridha is a leading shipper of jutes and we are in clined to believe the statement because it is stated that since his release on ad-interim bail he had exported jutes worth taka forty lacs and thereby earned the foreign exchange. He made profit in the business no doubt, but for the State he earned the foreign exchange. In this view we have now come to the irresistible conclusion that this proceeding must be quashed. We find support for this view in the observation made by the Supreme Courtin the case of MS Khawaja vs State reported in 17 DLR (SC) 153 ; which runs as follows :—
